#2779. Mike Vick, Norfolk State lose after his order was ignored

Like a growing number of former NFL players, Mike Vick has become a college football coach. Unlike many college football coaches, a direct order from Vick wasn’t followed on Saturday.

With 1:34 to play during Saturday’s game between Vick’s Norfolk State and North Carolina Central, Norfolk State led, 28-23. Norfolk State had the ball, facing second and five from the 50. North Carolina Central had no timeouts remaining.

While a pair of knees wouldn’t have fully exhausted the remaining time, Vick told the offense to take a knee in victory formation. Two straight kneel-downs would have resulted in a punt with less than 15 seconds to play.

Instead, Norfolk State lined up in shotgun formation, the quarterback ran to the left, a defender hit him, and the quarterback fumbled.

North Carolina Central recovered at the Norfolk State 37. Five plays later, North Carolina scored a touchdown, on a 26-yard touchdown pass, making the score 29-28. (The two-point conversion attempt failed.)

Twenty-seven seconds remained. Norfolk State drove in position to attempt a game-winning field goal. The 37-yard try missed wide left.

“I don’t know what happened at the end of the game,” Vick told reporters after a loss that dropped Norfolk State to 4-6 on the season. “I put my headset down. I called victory formation. All we had to do was take a knee, kneel the clock out. That’s just situational football. I don’t know what happened in regards to that. I looked up and we was running the ball, and then I seen the fumble. But my final instructions was victory formation. That’s when you kneel it out. And they had, I think, zero timeouts left and the game was over practically.”

“Well, I put my headset down, and I took my headset off because all we had to do was just run it three times, or two times, or kneel it out. That’s called victory. I don’t know what happened. A run play was called. I looked up, I seen us running the ball. I don’t know what happened. I really don’t. I don’t know what the play call was. I don’t know why we even ran that play.

“People will look at that, and that’ll go on as a teaching tape for a lot of teams across the country for years to come. I hate it had to be us. But I called victory formation. Just letting everybody know that. I called victory.”

While the strategy wouldn’t have completely exhausted the clock, it was the right move. And, even if it wasn’t, the coach gave the order. The order wasn’t followed.

So what happened? Vick said he had taken off his headset and then later realized that a run play had been called. The fact that the offense went straight into shotgun formation suggests that it wasn’t the players going rogue. Apparently, offensive coordinator Brian Sheppard decided to ignore Vick’s directive.

Indeed, a somewhat chaotic postgame video (posted by Vick on Twitter) includes Vick telling his players “it was supposed to have been victory.”

The video of the moments before the play in question shows the offense gathered at the numbers near the Norfolk State bench, speaking to a group of coaches who were still wearing headsets. The coach without a headset (who appears to be Vick) walked to the sideline before turning around and returning to the meeting.

It’s clear that the coaches and players were having a discussion. From Vick’s perspective, there was nothing to discuss.

And while Vick claims his instruction was ignored, he seemed to be a little too nonchalant at a time when he should have realized that something more detailed than telling the quarterback to line up under center, receive the snap, and take a knee was being planned.

If Vick believes Sheppard or other coaches overruled the head coach, Vick should be issuing pink slips immediately. It’s possible, though, that Vick himself bears the bulk of the blame for not noticing that something other than the implementation of victory formation was coming.

It was an inspired performance, particularly without the heartbeat of the defense, Jack Campbell. The Lions clearly dedicated the game to him, sporting No. 46 jerseys while walking into the stadium. And while Campbell vowed this week to eventually continue his NFL career, Detroit proved on Sunday that they can operate without him for now.

Here's a full recap of the Lions' 19-9 win over the Dolphins.

The Lions got the ball first and had great field position after the kickoff landed before the landing zone. Interestingly, it was Miles Frazier at left guard to start the game in place of the (presumably) healthy Christian Mahogany. After picking up 6 yards on the first two plays, Jared Goff and the Lions faced an quick third-and-4. Goff found Amon-Ra St. Brown for a nice gain of 16 yards between Dolphins' zone coverage defenders. Detroit failed to pick up the next third-and-short when Goff's arm was hit by Dolphins defender Josh Uche.

That set up a fourth-and-3 from the Dolphins' 31-yard line. Detroit went for it, and Goff avoided pressure to find Isaac TeSlaa for 8 to keep the drive alive. Then Jahmyr Gibbs took a wildcat snap, faked a pitch to Goff, and took it for 16 yards down to the Dolphins' 6-yard line.

But on third-and-goal, Goff was sacked by Uche, forcing the Lions to settled for a chip-shot field goal. 3-0 Lions.

Detroit managed to get a quick three-and-out on defense after two rushes went for 0 yards, and Malik Willis' third-down pass was too far for his receiver.

But the Lions quickly gave the ball back to Miami. After two successful runs, Goff's arm was hit again by Uche while throwing, and the ball went right to Dolphins defensive back Chris Johnson.

Miami moved into scoring position with a leaping grab from Caleb Douglas for 20 yards down to the Lions' 20-yard line. In the red zone, the Dolphins faced a third-and-11 and they tried to catch Detroit sleeping with a draw play. But Aidan Hutchinson sniffed it out for a short gain, and the Dolphins settled for a field goal to tie it up. 3-3 tie.

The Lions offense gained just 3 yards on their first two plays to set up a big third-and-7 to start the second quarter.

On the first play, Goff went deep to Jameson Williams, but the receiver bobbled a very catchable ball and the Lions were forced to punt…. or were they?!? Jack Fox drilled a pass to Tay Martin for the fake punt conversion and 11 yards.

Detroit had to dig themselves out of hole, though, as Frazier was called for a holding penalty on the next play. While an 11-yard pass to St. Brown helped, a failed screen set up a third-and-9. And on the play, the Dolphins sent an aggressive blitz and Miami picked up their third sack of the game. This time, the Lions did actually punt the ball away.

The Dolphins were pinned at their own 5-yard line, but a play-action pass to Greg Dulcich for 11 yards got Miami out of the jam. That said, Hutchinson drew a holding penalty that eventually set up a third-and-18 for the Dolphins. Pressure from the Lions forced Willis to throw it away.

Despite a holding penalty on the Lions on the punt, they still got great field position due to a shank from Dolphins punter Bradley Pinion. Detroit started on their own 43-yard line, hoping to put some of the offensive line issues behind them. The drive started promisingly with an 11-yard pass to Sam LaPorta and a 10-yard run from Gibbs. Two plays later, Goff hit St. Brown for another 14 yards.

However, the drive stalled from there. A toss to Gibbs lost 3 yards. Then another Gibbs run lost another 3 yards. Goff scrambled on third down to make the field goal a little shorter, and Bates drilled a 40-yard field goal to make it 6-3 Lions with 3:30 left in the half.

Miami responded before the half ended. A reverse to Kevin Coleman earned 16 yards and put the Dolphins in Lions territory. Ollie Gordon then got Miami into field goal range with a pair of draws that went for 9 and 11 yards. Eventually, Miami drove down to the Lions' 10-yard line and had a shot at the end zone. But Hutchinson drew another holding penalty, forcing the Dolphins to kick a game-tying field goal, but former Lions Zane Gonzalez missed a 38-yard field goal to keep it 6-3 Lions at halftime.

Miami started with the ball and picked up a quick first down thanks to a pass interference penalty on Derrick Barnes. He made amends with a tackle for loss on the next play, helping set up a third-and-11 for the Dolphins. Willis tried to force a ball into a tight window, but safety Chuck Clark picked it off and returned it all the way to the Dolphins 26-yard line.

Gibbs gave the Lions a new set of downs inside the red zone with a third-and-1 conversion with a 3-yard gain on a toss. However, the Lions had to settle for another field goal when a second down Gibbs run went for no gain and Sam LaPorta committed a false start to set up a third-and-11. Goff turfed a pass to Gibbs, and Bates was good from 33. 9-3 Lions.

Bates' ensuing kickoff was well short of the landing zone, setting the Dolphins up at the 40-yard line. Miami turned that into points. One key play was a third-and-11 pass to Douglas, who ran a 9-yard curl, then avoided a tackle attempt from Ennis Rakestraw to get the first down. Detroit drew another holding penalty—Skyler Gill-Howard this time. And it forced Miami to settle for another field goal attempt. This time Gonzalez was good from 52 yards. 9-6 Lions.

Detroit looked to retaliate quickly. A 31-yard strike to Jameson Williams immediately put the Lions in field goal position on the first play of the drive.

Goff hit St. Brown for 17 on the very next play, putting Detroit into the red zone. The Lions then faced a third-and-1, and the Dolphins were all over Detroit's play-action attempt. The Lions obviously went for it on fourth-and-1, and Detroit dialed up a well-timed pitch to Gibbs, who beat everyone to the outside for an 8-yard touchdown. 16-6 Lions.

Miami faced a third-and-3 at the start of the fourth quarter.

The Dolphins failed to convert after Malcolm Rodriguez punched out the ball on what would've been a converted first down pass. But Miami pulled off a fake punt of their own, and it was even more successful than Detroit's, gaining 46 yards.

Then, on a third-and-5 inside the red zone, Willis found Malik Washington for 7 yards to move the chain. Alim McNeill tallied a sack to put the Dolphins in a tough third-and-goal situation from the 13.

Derrick Moore chased down Willis on third down, forcing yet another field goal from the Dolphins. 16-9 Lions.

Detroit avoided a third-and-out when an attempt to St. Brown drew a 17-yard pass interference penalty. That would be all the Lions could muster, though. A holding penalty on Blake Miller pushed the Lions back, but Detroit dug out of it with a 17-yard screen to St. Brown on a third-and-8.

Detroit would stall out from there, as Goff overthrew St. Brown on third-and-7. Bates' 43-yard field goal was good, to give Detroit a two-score lead with 4:28 left. 19-9 Lions.

Starting at their own 35-yard line, the Dolphins had to score twice and score quickly. But Detroit's defensive line took over. Hutchinson forced a throw away on first down, Moore got a sack on second down, and on fourth-and-12, the Dolphins dropped a potential conversion. Detroit took over at Miami's 33 with 3:02 left and the game in hand.

The Lions offense managed to earn a couple of first downs and bleed the rest of the clock to move to 6-2 on the season at the midway point of the year.

#2775. Sixers visit Bulls for second meeting in Sunday matinee

The Philadelphia 76ers have one more game on this road trip before they head home, visiting the Chicago Bulls on Sunday afternoon.

This is the second time in under a week the Sixers and Bulls are meeting, with the Sixers winning their first foray 126-107 back on Monday. With the Bulls going into that contest 1-5, some may have expected the then 6-1 Sixers to have handled that game with ease… but it took until the final few minutes for Philadelphia to finally pull away from Chicago. Since then, the Bulls have dropped to 1-7 on the season, and come into Sunday on a six-game skid.

Looking at the injury reports, Joel Embiid is currently probable for Sunday's contest due to plantar fasciitis management. Not sure if it was what was bothering him on Friday, but he certainly seemed off in that one to say the least. And the hits just keep coming at the center position for Philadelphia with Adem Bona ruled out for a second consecutive game due to a cervical spine sprain. This may mean that — for better or worse —there's more pressure on Embiid to play even if he isn't 100% right now. The only other injury note for the Sixers are that Dominick Barlow (back) remains out.

For the Bulls, there is some mystery around who may be playing center for them tomorrow as well. Nic Claxton is currently listed as questionable after being sidelined to start the season with a hamstring strain. Him being listed as questionable is a step toward the direction of the Bulls' starting center possibly taking the floor against the Sixers. Jalen Smith, who has been starting at the five in Claxton's absence, is probable with a left finger sprain. Also for Chicago, Tobe Awaka is questionable while Zach Collins and Dailyn Swain are out.

The Bulls will have the rest advantage this afternoon as they haven't played since Wednesday for some unknown reason. Who am I to question the wisdom of the NBA schedule makers?

Earlier this week, the Sixers utilized a widespread effort across their starters to get the job done against the Bulls. All five starters scored in the double-digits, and three scored more than 20 points each. It was an especially impressive night from VJ Edgecombe, who shot 9-for-12 from the floor and 2-for-4 from behind the arc for 21 points. Tyrese Maxey had a 26-point, 11 assist double-double, Jaylen Brown added a 25-point, 11-rebound double-double, and LeBron James posted 15 points and nine assists — some of which were just incredible displays of playmaking.

I'm a big believer in "if it ain't broke, don't fix it". One of the things the Sixers did exceptionally well in that contest was getting out in transition on a clinical level. A shot would go up on the defensive end, James would be ready to rebound as Edgecombe or Maxey preemptively charged up the floor. A few incredible, quarterback-level passes from James and the Sixers enjoyed the benefits of taking the easy buckets as they came.

That last part is my advice for the Sixers tonight: don't make it harder than it needs to be. Take the easy buckets out in stride when you can get them. Don't let the Bulls grab offensive rebound after offensive rebound for second chance points. Don't rely on one player to do all the heavy lifting. Spread the floor and the ball, and don't turn it into a battle to the end with a team that is objectively worse. If you can, get a lead big enough that even Nick Nurse gives the starting five a little rest toward the end.

Coming off just their second loss of the season, one can imagine the Sixers coming into Sunday with a strong desire to right the ship. Right there with them is a Bulls squad that is desperately trying to find their footing this season and may have their starting center back in the mix. Regardless, this is one that the Sixers really should win, barring any major changes to the injury reports pregame.

But we all know how well "should" goes in the NBA.

The Sixers and Bulls tip off at 3:30 p.m. ET.

#2771. Palace consider replacing Sage, with Frank among contenders

Crystal Palace manager Pierre Sage is in serious danger of losing his job only five months into his reign, with the club bottom of the Premier League going into the international break.

Sunday's 3-1 defeat by Liverpool was Palace's fourth successive league loss, with Sage's side having won just two of their 10 league matches this season.

The club have held internal talks aimed at deciding Sage's future and his potential successor.

Former Tottenham and Brentford manager Thomas Frank is viewed as a strong candidate, while ex-Nottingham Forest boss Sean Dyche also has some support internally.

Both are out of work and would be available to start immediately.

Palace have taken just seven points from their 10 league matches and have the worst defensive record in the league, having conceded 24 goals.

They are also 21st in the Europa League, currently enough for a play-off spot, with only one win from their four matches.

If he is dismissed, Frenchman Sage could become the first managerial casualty of the Premier League season.

He was appointed on a three-year contract in June after Oliver Glasner departed at the end of last season.

"It's not from the dream to the nightmare," the 47-year-old said after the defeat by Liverpool.

"I'm not feeling this. I'm just in my job, and focusing on my job, and what I have to do to find the solution.

"The results are not at this level, and I know I have to push more on those things, especially in our way of playing, to make that move."

Sage previously led Lens to a second-place finish in Ligue 1 and a first French Cup triumph in their 120-year history.

However, he has been unable to replicate Glasner's success at Palace. Glasner, who now manages Nottingham Forest, led Palace to a first FA Cup title and a Europa Conference League triumph.

Palace are winless in the league since 11 October, with their losing run sparked by a 5-0 loss to fierce rivals Brighton.

After that match, Sage said he felt "shame" and admitted he did not know if he would be given time to turn Palace's fortunes around.

However, there was a degree of sympathy from some behind the scenes.

Injuries were not kind to his plans, while the absence of Jean-Philippe Mateta and Ismaila Sarr - due to a mixture of fitness and personal issues, related to both players' desire to leave the club - did not help the start of his reign.

However, three more league defeats have followed, with Palace hitting the bar and having a goal ruled out in their loss to Liverpool at Selhurst Park.

"We have to be more competitive," Sage said on Sunday.

"At the moment, we create some things, we expect a lot of things, but we don't have the results expected."

#2765. Winston, McCarthy combine to lead Giants to 19-11 win and hand Eagles 7th straight loss

PHILADELPHIA (AP) — Jameis Winston replaced the injured J.J. McCarthy long enough to throw a go-ahead touchdown pass and help the New York Giants keep their grip on the NFC East and beat Philadelphia 19-11 on Sunday to hand the Eagles their seventh straight loss.

The Eagles (2-7) are on their longest losing streak since they lost eight straight games in Andy Reid's final season in 2012.

With Jalen Hurts likely out for the season with blood clots and a playoff berth all but gone, the Eagles could get a roster makeover at Tuesday's NFL trade deadline.

The Giants (5-2-1) are the only team in the division with a winning record.

The Eagles had beaten the Giants 13 straight times at home — including one playoff win — since New York last won on Oct. 27, 2013.

It doesn't seem to matter who's playing quarterback for the Giants.

McCarthy suffered a hip injury in the third quarter that briefly forced him out of the game and the Giants trailing 8-6.

Coach John Harbaugh turned to Winston — who held the starting job for four games after No. 1 QB Jaxson Dart was injured — to rally New York.

Winston did enough in his cameo to keep New York's first division title since 2011 within reach. He hit wide receiver Malachi Fields for 14 yards that took the ball to the Eagles 3-yard line and followed two plays later with a 5-yard TD pass to Isaiah Likely that sent the Giants into the fourth quarter with a 13.-8 lead.

McCarthy returned for the final play of the third quarter. He completed 12 of 19 passes for 127 yards and no touchdowns or interceptions. Winston was 6 of 8 for 71 yards and the lone touchdown.

Dominic Zvada kicked field goals of 53 and 49 yards for a 6-0 lead in the first quarter and connected from 38 and 49 yards in the second half for a 19-8 lead.

Like the Giants, the Eagles have also cycled through quarterbacks because of injuries and ineffectiveness.

Tanner McKee went 0-3 since taking over for Hurts as the starter before he was benched this week for Joe Milton.

The 26-year-old Milton had appeared in five NFL games in relief and was suddenly tasked with saving the Eagles' season.

He showed flashes of the speed and strong arm that McKee doesn't have. Like McKee. Milton couldn't do much to move the offense.

Saquon Barkley scored on a 3-yard run late in the first quarter and — after a Giants penalty on the extra point — Milton ran in for the 2-point conversion for an 8-7 lead. Milton punctuated the score with a backflip in the end zone that got a rise out of the crowd.

Milton went 18 of 34 for 169 yards and was sacked on the final play of the game. Jake Elliott added a 45-yard field goal.

Jonathan Greenard finally got his first sack as an Eagle after he was acquired from Minnesota in a draft-weekend trade. The edge rusher subsequently agreed to a four-year, $98 million extension, including $50 million guaranteed.

Braden Mann unleashed an 86-yard punt for the Eagles at the end of the first half. It was the longest punt in the NFL since 2001. Mann punted out of the end zone (the ball was spotted at the Eagles 8) and rolled out of bounds at the Giants 6-yard line.

Mann followed with a 60-yarder to end the Eagles' first drive of the second half. He also lost 2 yards on a botched punt.

Former Eagles quarterback Randall Cunningham actually holds the franchise record with a 91-yarder in 1989.

Eagles head into a bye and return on Nov. 22 to host the Steelers.

#2760. Eagles-Giants instant analysis: Quarterback change cannot fix offense

The Eagles changed the quarterback without changing the central problem. Their offense still could not produce enough consistent gains to support a defense that gave them a legitimate chance to win.

Sunday's 19-11 loss to the Giants pushed Philadelphia to 2-7, extending a losing streak that has swallowed a 2-0 start. Joe Milton supplied movement, a few extended plays and an early celebration, but the Eagles finished with 220 yards and one touchdown. The evidence pointed toward problems that reach beyond the player taking the snap.

Milton rushed for 64 yards on nine attempts, accounting for most of Philadelphia's 92 rushing yards. His 19-yard first-half scramble extended the touchdown drive, and his mobility created gains that weren't available within the original structure of several plays.

That contribution mattered. It also exposed how little the conventional offense generated. Saquon Barkley and Elijah Mitchell combined for 28 yards on 16 carries, leaving Milton to create too much of the rushing production himself.

New York collected seven sacks and 11 quarterback hits, with Arvell Reese responsible for three sacks and a forced fumble. Philadelphia lost 41 yards on sacks, reducing Milton's 169 passing yards to 128 net passing yards.

Those losses repeatedly turned difficult possessions into nearly impossible ones. The Eagles need to evaluate protection assignments, individual execution, and the quarterback's responses together. Assigning every sack to one cause would miss the larger breakdown.

Philadelphia held New York to 243 yards and 2.6 yards per rushing attempt while collecting six sacks. The Giants' starting running back, Devin Singletary, needed 21 carries to gain 31 yards.

The defense was not flawless. Winston's touchdown pass to Isaiah Likely exposed a damaging red-zone coverage breakdown. Still, allowing 19 points while generating that much disruption should have given Philadelphia a workable path.

The Eagles scored eight points in the first quarter and three over the final three periods. They converted five of 18 third downs and failed twice on fourth down.

Milton's athleticism gives the coaching staff something to develop. That doesn't excuse an offense that cannot consistently protect, run, or stay ahead of the chains. Philadelphia needs a plan that creates repeatable gains instead of depending on its quarterback to rescue broken possessions.

The Cavaliers beat the Knicks on Saturday, adding another win to their analytical spreadsheet.

On giving Landry Shamet more leeway than younger reserves and keeping bench minutes competitive:

"Obviously, you looking at a guy like Landry, he may have a little bit more leash than Pac [Dadiet]. Landry's as close to being a starter as you can imagine for us. Everybody else, they have to play and even the starters and Landry, they do, too."

On Landry Shamet's standing in the Knicks' rotation:

"About as close to being a starter as you can imagine for us."

On choosing Tyler Kolek over Jose Alvarado as the backup point guard:

"But you know, Jose had the first opportunity [against the Nets) and then I gave Tyler an opportunity in the second half and Tyler played well. So I go with Tyler and if I feel I need to make a change, Tyler's not getting it done in my eyes, I'll go back to Jose."

On Josh Hart's ability to contribute without having plays called for him:

"Josh is a connector. I don't think we call a single play for him at any time, he just goes and gets it done.

"He rebounds. Our pick and roll defense has been bad, and he's helped clean it up at times by putting him on the ball. So his versatility defensively is a bonus for us. So he's definitely going to be missed."

On facing Cleveland again after defeating the Cavaliers in the Eastern Conference finals:

On acknowledging that he underestimated Taylor Swift's history as a Knicks fan:

On the reaction to his comments about Taylor Swift and admitting he answered the question poorly:

On being a Taylor Swift fan despite questioning her Knicks fandom:

"I love her music. I probably know more songs than anybody else in the locker room. I just misspoke."

On returning to Cleveland and remembering the Knicks' championship run:

"It's human nature, you're gonna revert back and think back to the last time you were in the building. I had a quick little firing of that walking in for shootaround, but I think the general sense was that was last year. That was great. You can have those memories and hang on to that as long as we want, but ultimately this year is a new year and a new endeavor."

On the benefits of roster continuity and familiarity with Mike Brown:

"The biggest thing is just being comfortable with the guys on the floor, second year with [head coach] Mike [Brown]. I think that just breeds confidence. Familiarity breeds confidence. There's no denying that. It allows you to get to the point of conversations quicker. It makes for a good formula to find success."

On comparing his unpredictable Knicks role to that of a baseball relief pitcher:

"Especially with [my] role, I think I take a lot from my buddy Ashby, bullpen guy, you don't know when you're gonna get thrown in, what the situation's gonna be. My job might look a little different from night to night. If I'm changing my approach every night, that's not setting myself up for a good situation.

"I think in the past in my career when I was younger I would try to overcomplicate things and think I have to reinvent the wheel. I try to just keep it as simple as possible, reduce it down to my job, my impact and just play my game."

On Cleveland's Saturday loss to the Knicks:

"No excuse. These are games that we feel like we should win. We got another tough stretch coming up so there's no reason to sit here and feel bad and nothing's won in the first 10 games."

"I think we just gave them too many second-chance opportunities. Then it's too late, you're down 20 trying to fight back, but it's too late."

On the Cavaliers failing to match the Knicks' intensity:

"Got to bring your A game and we just didn't do that tonight."

On Cleveland continuing to compete despite trailing New York by 18 points:

On acknowledging that the Knicks dominated the Cavaliers in the Eastern Conference finals and then won the championship:

"They dominated it, and they did it again against San Antonio [in the Finals]. Analytically … there's an 'expected score,' and we've won two out of the three games.

"I think when you look back on it and take the context of the question, I'm not sure that was taken into account, which I know was a little bit of a lesson for me — like, you can just take a sound bite (and run with it).

"I would just say there was no coach more complimentary of the Knicks and honest about our performance and how they dominated us. So you live and learn a little bit with those things. But like I said, 99 percent of my comments were how they dominated us. They were by far the better team. I answered the question, as it was taken, (which was) 'And you're down 3-0, what hope do you have of even giving to your guys?'

On why analytics could not outweigh the Knicks' physical and mental dominance:

"We get information that checks our process. All that being said, we were still dominated. It kind of doesn't matter (what the analytics say) because there is more than that. There is the mental toughness, the physical toughness, the flow to the game, how aggressive you are. There are all these other intangibles that go with that."

On recognizing that the Knicks earned their championship:

"They deserved it, and they did it again against San Antonio. Just an incredible, incredible run."

#2754. What did we learn from Shedeur Sanders' start vs. Saints? Instant reaction

NEW ORLEANS ― The Browns won a game where the quarterback spent most of it struggling to find consistency. Then, in the fourth quarter, found a way to make a play.

That had been the wasy Deshaun Watson had been quarterbacking the Browns to five wins in their first eight games. However, with Watson inactive as he returned from a concussion, Shedeur Sanders made his first start of the season at the New Orleans Saints.

However, for most of the game, the story of the game was both teams' inability to turn opportunities into touchdowns. They came alive in the final six minutes of regulation and then into overtime for what ended up being a 23-22 overtime loss to the Saints.

The first of four touchdowns and one field goal in the final six minutes came when Sanders hit wide receiver KC Concepcion for a 62-yard touchdown with 5:41 remaining. That was one of two 60-plus-yard completions for Sanders, who also had a 60-yarder to Denzel Boston that ultimately only netted a field goal.

Sanders also had a great throw to Jerry Jeudy on the drive that ended with Andre Szmyt's overtime-forcing 51-yard field goal with eight seconds left in regulation. That was one of three regulation field goals for Szmyt.

The Saints, though, scored touchdowns on their last true regulation possession and only overtime possession. The Browns scored on Harold Fannin Jr.'s wild 39-yard catch-and-run in overtime, but couldn't convert what would've been the game-winning two-point converion.

Here are our instant thoughts and reactions immediately after the clock hit all zeros.

Sanders, for the first three quarters, played like a backup quarterback who received practice reps for three days and then had a walkthrough the day before the game. Which isn't so much a shot as it is a reality for a backup.

Then the fourth quarter and overtime happened and he came alive. He finished 19-of-31 for 297 yards with two touchdowns, after starting 7-of-12 for 100 yards over the first three quarters.

The second-year pro seemed, at times, a tad tentative as he was catching back up to the speed of a real game. That's not to say that there weren't moments, but there was never a sense of any consistency in the play.

Take the Browns' two trips inside the Saints 10, one on each side of halftime. Both times they got there, Sanders immediately got sacked to set them back.

The first one ended with a fourth-down stop by the Saints. The second one, set up by a big throw to Denzel Boston for 60 yards ended with an Andre Szmyt field goal.

The Browns had penalties in all three phases by the time each of them had had a chance to be on the field. They had penalties in all four quarters, with all three phases contributing to the issue.

By the end of the game, the Browns had nine penalties for 53 yards. They had allowed New Orleans to get two first downs because of them.

More than anything, they just continue to show a lack of discipline that still exists. They lead the NFL in penalties, which is unacceptable for any team.

The biggest catch of the game for the Browns may have been the one Jerry Jeudy made on the Browns sideline with former Browns cornerback M.J. Emerson in tight coverage. It was a 30-yarder that put Cleveland at the Saints 40.

That eventually led to the Szmyt game-tying 51-yard field goal with eight seconds remaining. Meaning, Jeudy once again had one of his few catches keep a critical drive going.

Jeudy had three combined catches between the home wins over the Pittsburgh Steelers and the Baltimore Ravens that help on key game-winning drive. This one wasn't on a winning drive, but the Browns avoided a regulation loss because of it.

The Browns allowed the Saints to move the ball at will throughout the game. Yet another terrible run game ran all over them, while a mid passing game suddenly was prolific.

The Saints needed a touchdown with less than two minutes left? Effortless. They needed to take the opening kick of overtime and move it down the field? Not a problem.

The Browns defense had its share of plays over the course of the afternoon. That's why New Orleans only had one regulation touchdown.

However, they weren't able to make a bad offense look bad. Instead, much like the Tennessee Titans, they looked as good as they have all season.

The victory moves the Chiefs to 6-2 on the season and Walker is now tied with Jahmyr Gibbs for the league lead with 11 total touchdowns on the season.

It’s the fifth multi-touchdown game of Walker’s first season with the Chiefs and the Chiefs have won all of those games. He did not score in either of their losses, so his importance to the offense probably can’t be overstated.

Walker ran 18 times for 102 yards and his four catches picked up 41 yards, which gave him more yards from scrimmage on Sunday than he managed in either of the Chiefs’ two losses.

The Chiefs got a scare just before halftime when Patrick Mahomes hurt his right elbow on a sack by Jets first-rounder David Bailey. The Chiefs lost a fumble on the play, but Mahomes was able to remain in the game and no negative impact on his game was visible over the second half. Mahomes finished 23-of-31 for 242 yards and four of those completions went to Travis Kelce for 72 yards. Kelce also had a one-yard rushing touchdown.

Mahomes and Kelce have been joined on the top line of Chiefs stars by defensive tackle Chris Jones for many years and Jones chipped in a pair of sacks of Jets quarterback Geno Smith during the win. George Karlaftis had a pair of them as well and the Chiefs will try to keep things firing on all cylinders in Atlanta next Sunday.

One change they could make is with kicker Harrison Butker. He missed another field goal and Justin Tucker is on the practice squad, so the team could opt for a new kicker against the Falcons.

Smith was sacked five times . The Jets actually controlled much of the first half and had chances to put points on the board, but had to settle for five field goal tries. Jason Sanders made four of those kicks, but the Jets needed touchdowns that never came.

They will host the Bills next Sunday and the 2-7 team figures to hear a lot more chatter about Aaron Glenn’s job security in the wake of their fourth straight loss. Five of their first six losses were one-score games, but getting outscored 21-0 in the second half on Sunday doesn’t make much of a case for Glenn having the team on the right path.

#2752. Cowboys beat Colts in thriller as Caleb Downs seals it

The Dallas Cowboys were the winning team on Sunday in Indianapolis, but goodness did they make it more difficult than it had to be.

The fourth quarter was full of all sorts of chaos and near the end of it things were very dark.

To be clear, the fact that the game was this close against a team of Indianapolis' caliber, what with how they have already begun to sell off assets, is representative of an important takeaway on the macro level. But the Cowboys won, they are now 4-5, and they are still well alive in their quest to accomplish their goals this season.

This was a win that the Cowboys needed in the worst way and so perhaps it will serve as a catalyst moving forward. Still, lessons can be learned as noted.

Perhaps the Cowboys will feel that what happened was enough to be active during the coming week's trade deadline action. We will see.

The Colts won the toss and deferred which put the Cowboys offense at work first. Given that George Pickens was inactive for the game there was some holding of breath involved.

An early third down conversion to Jonathan Mingo suggested that things were going to go well for the Cowboys. They stalled right after that though, but they were close enough (thanks to the Colts kicking it out of bounds to start the game) to be in field goal range and Brandon Aubrey's 45-yard attempt was good. Dallas led 3-0.

You will never believe it, but the defense pitched a three and out right after. Early on the game was starting as well as it possibly could have.

It was then that things turned. Two plays after the Cowboys got the ball back they were facing a third down… and Dak Prescott got caught from behind. The ball popped loose, Indy recovered, and they suddenly very much in business.

A few moments later… the Colts were in the endzone and had taken a 7-3 lead.

The Cowboys ran the ball amid a bunch of penalties on the next drive and took things all the way to the end of the quarter.

The second quarter began with Dallas facing a 3rd and 1 from the Indianapolis 9-yard line.

On 3rd-and-1 Brian Schottenheimer called a bit of a trick play where Dak Prescott pitched it to an in-motion CeeDee Lamb. This seemed like doing way too much and Lamb lost yardage.

Dallas rolled the dice on fourth down, though. All was looking lost and then Prescott found Jake Ferguson in the back of the endzone for a huge score. Serious props to Ferguson for fighting the sun in his eyes and for having strong enough hands to hold on.

One of the benefits of this drive was that it took a really long time which allowed the Cowboys defense to get some serious rest. They responded by capitalizing on that with their second three-and-out of the game. Unfortunately the Cowboys had their own which gave Indy the ball right back.

The game saw its third straight three and out, but this one had some pop to it. As the Colts were trying to make magic on third down… Caleb Downs said absolutely not with his second sack of the season.

It turned into a bunch of nothing for the Cowboys, though. Tyler Goodson converted on the first play of the possession so it was not another three-and-out, but Dallas failed to pick up a second down right away so it was as close as possible without actually being one. The Cowboys remained in the lead 10-7 and with half of the second quarter remaining and Indy set to receive the ball after halftime… it felt like a game-defining possession.

It was yet another three-and-out for Indy, although just barely as Laquon Treadwell made a heroic catch on third down where his feet were ruled to be out of bounds. Still they punted.

This marked the fourth time in the game that the Cowboys defense gave the offense the ball off of a stop. No points were scored off of the first three so putting a stop to that was obviously important.

As important as it was… it did not happen. Penalties derailed a drive where Dallas was legitimately moving the ball, although on plays that wound up getting wiped out. The Cowboys punted and the Colts took over with 2:11 left in the half.

They were unable to do anything yet again. Dallas burned a timeout at one point to preserve the clock and took over at their own 25-yard line with 49 seconds left and two timeouts in their pocket. Everybody was curious what they were going to turn it into.

With the Cowboys in some long distance field goal range they did what they did not do last week and tried CeeDee Lamb deep. This makes sense because, you know, he's CeeDee Lamb.

That about did it and the Cowboys took a 17-7 lead into the locker room for halftime.

The first half theme continued for Indianapolis as their offense sputtered to start after the break. It was another three-and-out.

Unfortunately so was Dallas' possession. This marked the sixth time that the offense got the ball off of a defensive stop and the fifth time that they did nothing with it.

Finally, someone put together a drive. It was Indianapolis who put together the first double-digit play drive since Dallas' first touchdown of the game. Thankfully they only squeaked out a field goal as a result of it all, but they narrowed things down to a one-possession game at 17-10.

Points were absolutely vital on the next possession and they acted like it. CeeDee Lamb got things going and almost had a touchdown, but he was unable to keep both feet in bounds. Dallas did scored, but it was by way of a Brandon Aubrey field goal which took things back to a two-score lead at 20-10.

That score did not last long, though. The Cowboys defense had been doing such a great job at holding… but they were never going to pitch a perfect game. Daniel Jones found Ashton Dulin and it was over.

This was suddenly a 20-17 game with just a little bit left in the third quarter. It felt a like like the way the third quarter ended last week, to be honest. This one did officially end with Dallas driving to try and put the game away.

It appeared as if the Cowboys did indeed put an end to the game. Kind of.

Dak Prescott found CeeDee Lamb with pressure in his face which was impressive enough. Lamb was able to miraculously field the pass that was underthrown as a result of the pressure, and even more amazingly he realized that he was not down by contact.

CeeDee proceeded to get up, with all sorts of chaos and franticness happening around him, and picked up an extra chunk of yardage. Unfortunately as he finally came to the ground he fumbled and Indianapolis recovered.

It took a Colts challenge to rule that Lamb did indeed fumble, but they won it and Indy took over.

All of a sudden the Colts were moving with energy. DaRon Bland got called for a pass interference penalty after they had already developed some positive momentum, and it was suddenly starting to feel very scary for Dallas.

But then a hero entered and his name was Quinnen Williams. He quite literally snatched victory from the jaws of defeat by forcing a fumble that Shemar James was able to recover.

It should be noted that Dallas was backed up to start due to DeMarvion Overshown running onto the field to celebrate the turnover. You would think there would be a little more awareness going on in situations like this, but I digress.

The Cowboys were yet again unable to do anything with a stop generated by their defense and they punted the ball back to Indianapolis.

Indy took advantage this time. They got within long-distance field goal range and converted a 59-yard attempt to tie the game. Dallas took over with things square at 20 with just under six minutes left.

It took two and a half minutes, but the Cowboys got into field goal range themselves and were forced to take it. The attempt for Brandon Aubrey was from 50 yards out… and he pulled it left. Notably the broadcast showed that the snap bounced off of the ground, but he was able to cleanly attempt it. This left the Colts over three minutes to work with the game tied at 20.

The Cowboys burned all of their timeouts in an effort to preserve time to try to answer whatever the Colts did. ON 3rd and 8 the Colts tried to find Josh Downs to move the chains and Caleb Downs helped force the incompletion. You can't write this stuff.

Indianapolis did convert a field goal after the fact though and took the lead late, 23-20. The Cowboys took over with 1:37 left and no timeouts to their name. It was on GOTI.

Right away… they delivered. Dak Prescott found Ryan Flournoy to put the Cowboys in field goal range and emotions were everywhere.

Shortly after… Flournoy even drew a pass interference penalty while in the endzone. He was a hero down the stretch.

With the field position what it was, the Colts very clearly let Javonte Williams walk into the endzone to preserve time themselves. Dallas took the lead again, 27-23, with 1:08 left and Indy still held two timeouts.

An early intentional grounding penalty put the Colts behind early, and then they had to press.

As they did… Caleb Downs sealed the deal with his first career interception!

Coming off an opening NBA Cup win against the Sacramento Kings, the Spurs faced a SEGABABA against the Portland Trail Blazers. After a sluggish first quarter, the Spurs, behind by 42 points in the second quarter, built their two-point lead to 15 at halftime. The Blazers simply could not stop the ball movement and three-point barrage by the silver and black, as the Spurs ultimately won 125-103.

Victor Wembanyama continues his early MVP campaign with another efficient high-scoring game of 29 points (9-13 FG, 3-6 3PT, 8-9 FT), seven rebounds, three assists, a block, and a steal. Despite only playing 24 minutes and not being as big a focal point of the offense as he was against Dallas and Sacramento, Wemby once again demonstrated how unguardable he truly is. Since he's shown he can shoot threes, Donovan Clingan steps out to guard him but immediately gets beat by Wemby on the drive to the basket. All Toumani Camara can do is go straight up, but against a seven-foot-four (he's definitely taller) alien, it's almost pointless.

The bulk of Wemby's scoring comes from inside the paint. He is dunking the ball more than any other player in the league and is even leading other TEAMS in total dunks. Where do most of his dunks come from? Lobs, of course.

#2748. Chase Briscoe’s 2026 NASCAR Season Ends in Heartbreak After Engine Failure at Homestead

Chase Briscoe's hopes of ending the 2026 NASCAR Cup Series season on a high note came to a sudden, devastating end Sunday at Homestead-Miami Speedway.

The Joe Gibbs Racing driver was running competitively in the season finale when his No. 19 Toyota suffered an engine failure late in Stage 1. Smoke poured from the car as Briscoe slowed on the track, bringing out the caution and ultimately ending the opening stage under yellow.

There would be no recovery for Briscoe, whose afternoon ended after just 78 laps of the scheduled 267-lap race.

The mechanical failure also had major championship implications. With Briscoe eliminated from contention, Kyle Larson secured the 2026 Cup Series title, even as the race itself continued.

For Briscoe, it was an especially frustrating ending considering how competitive his car had been before the failure.

Briscoe had shown promising speed throughout the opening stage, leading 33 laps and running among the frontrunners before trouble struck.

After climbing out of his Toyota, the 31-year-old made clear that the performance of the car wasn't the problem.

"No. We were really good there pace-wise," Briscoe said when asked about the failure.

He acknowledged noticing a warning sign before the engine gave way.

"A little bit of a vibration," he explained.

The failure was particularly difficult to accept because Briscoe believed he had a legitimate opportunity to compete for the victory.

"Super unfortunate. Felt like we were gonna be in the mix," he said.

Instead, his No. 19 Toyota was officially out of the race, leaving Briscoe to watch the remainder of the season finale from the sidelines.

The caution caused by his engine failure also brought Stage 1 to an early conclusion, interrupting a race that had already featured several changes for the lead.

Although Briscoe entered Sunday's finale already eliminated from championship contention, he still had plenty to race for. His No. 19 Toyota showed the speed to compete near the front, making the mechanical failure all the more frustrating.

The timing was particularly unfortunate for Joe Gibbs Racing, which still had two drivers, Denny Hamlin and Christopher Bell, mathematically capable of challenging Kyle Larson for the championship.

For Briscoe, however, the disappointment was more personal. After leading 33 laps and showing the potential to contend for the win, he was left wondering what might have been.

Despite the abrupt ending, Briscoe took a moment during his post-race interview to express his appreciation for Toyota and those who supported him throughout the season.

It wasn't the farewell to 2026 he had envisioned. Instead of fighting for a victory in the final race of the year, Briscoe was forced to watch from the sidelines as the championship battle continued without him.

#2747. Giants get first win in Philadelphia since 2013

Sunday’s performance in Philadelphia wasn’t a work of art for the Giants, but it was more than good enough to end their long losing streak in the City of Brotherly Love.

Tight end Isaiah Likely’s touchdown catch in the third quarter gave the Giants their first lead since the first quarter and they expanded it to 19-11 before punting the ball back to the Eagles with 90 seconds left to play in the game. Joe Milton picked up first downs on completions to Hollywood Brown and Dallas Goedert, but rookie wideout Makai Lemon dropped a pass that would have moved them into Giants territory and running back Elijah Mitchell didn’t get out of bounds on a short catch on the next play.

Milton spiked the ball with six seconds left to play and the Eagles on their own 44-yard-line for one final heave. Milton famously uncorked a 70-yard throw at the Combine, but he never got a chance to throw the ball because he was sacked by defensive end Darius Alexander.

That was one of seven Giants sacks on the afternoon, including three from first-round pick Arvell Reese. It was Reese’s first road game against the Eagles and his 1-0 record in Philly is a big change from recent history. The Giants had lost 13 straight games in Philadelphia and the route to ending that skid featured some strange twists and turns.

Likely’s touchdown catch came on a throw from Jameis Winston, who replaced J.J. McCarthy after McCarthy hurt his hip in the third quarter. Winston played one full series and threw for 71 yards on his way to the touchdown, but McCarthy returned just before the end of the quarter and led the offense for the rest of the proceedings.

McCarthy was sacked five times, but was 12-of-19 for 127 yards when he had time to throw and he ran for 22 yards while evading pressure over the course of the afternoon. The Giants couldn’t find any other success on the ground and Sunday’s 243 yards of offense didn’t make a strong case for the Giants sitting out the trade deadline if they have a chance to acquire any kind of help for their backfield.

Wide receiver Malik Nabers had five catches for 43 yards, but dropped a pass in the end zone that would have iced the win and his body language was that of an unhappy player throughout the game. The win should make it easier to avoid it being a focal point for the team after the game, but Nabers will likely have to answer some questions about what was bugging him.

They’ll be back on the field Thursday night against the Commanders and another win would move them to 6-2-1 with a 3-0-1 record in the division. That would make them even heavier favorites to win an NFC East that is theirs for the taking.

The Eagles spent a lot of time in that position in recent years, but injuries have gutted the roster and Milton didn’t provide any significant upgrade on the offensive production that the team got with Tanner McKee at quarterback. The Eagles will have a bye week to determine which way they want to go in the future, but the 2-7 team should really only have eyes on 2027 at this point.

#2745. Pistons vs Lakers preview: Best Defense vs best offense

Does it get any better than the No. 1 offense versus the No. 1 defense? The Detroit Pistons find themselves in that matchup as the 122-point-per-game Los Angeles Lakers visit Motown tonight.

Luka Dončić and the Lakers put up plenty of buckets, but scoring on Detroit is still an impossible task. The Pistons only surrender 101 points a game. Smothering defense every night.

Detroit's defense has its biggest test of the season if Dončić suits up this evening. He's questionable with lower back tightness.

It would be a shame if we're robbed of Cade Cunningham going head-to-head with another MVP candidate. The bigger shame would be if we miss out on Dončić versus Ausar Thompson. That matchup is like Jerry Rice versus Deion Sanders with how both are operating.

Detroit hasn't played since Wednesday's loss to the Philadelphia 76ers. They've had plenty of time to rest up. They'll need it if Dončić suits up.

Dončić is averaging 40 points. He's shooting 42% on nearly 14 3s a game. He gets to the line more than anybody. It's basically no stopping Dončić at the moment. This is a Wilt Chamberlain-like hot streak. Those two are the only players to average 40 nine games into the season. Whew, to say he's balling is an understatement.

But tasks like this are why the Pistons employ Ausar Thompson. If *anybody* can slow Dončić down, it's the best perimeter defender on the planet. Dončić usually has success against quick defenders with wiry strength, but Ausar is bigger and stronger this season. We'll be keeping tabs on how Ausar takes Dončić's bumps tonight. Ausar has the quick hands to disrupt things as well.

This might be a game where we see Paul Reed getting to the level and blitzing a bunch. J.B. Bickerstaff may decide to get the ball out of Dončić's hands and force someone else to beat them. Reed is capable of coming to the level on screens and muddying things up.

I'm sure Dončić will see some Cade tonight too. Cade won't make it easy with his sturdy frame. On the other end, the Lakers only have a few perimeter defenders to throw at Cade.

Matisse Thybulle is firmly in LA's rotation as he's started all 10 games. He's still a defensive playmaking threat. Cade deals with defenders like this nightly, but Thybulle is a plus defender nonetheless. So is Ziaire Williams. The springy 25-year-old treats every possession as if he'll never get in the game again if he doesn't go hard.

Those two are solid defensively, and Jake LaRavia competes. Outside of that, Detroit will have plenty of favorable matchups (Walker Kessler is a great rim protector and is off to a good offensive start. He can make a difference).

Dončić displays effort and is trying to shake the terrible defender narrative on his name, but attacking him is still the best way to slow him down. Make him work and keep him involved in actions.

Austin Reaves falls into the same boat. He's under Dončić on the Lakers' best defenders on the team list. Anybody with that matchup should look to be aggressive.

Reaves spends most of his time covering shooting guards. Will JJ Redick make Reaves chase Duncan Robinson all night? That's probably not ideal. Robinson runs even great defenders into the ground.

Robinson's light-em-up stretch continues as he's fourth in 3s made (35). Only Dončić, Nickeil Alexander-Walker, and Steph Curry have made more.

Detroit is letting it fly from deep as a team. According to Cleaning the Glass, 40 percent of their shots are coming from 3 (15th) compared to 31 percent last year (29th). Their rim rate has flipped the other way, but getting Jalen Duren back should rectify that.

The best offense versus the best defense is a mandatory viewing appointment. Can Ausar slow down the MVP-favorite? Do the Pistons show why they're an elite defense and smother Dončić as a team? Does Cade deliver a masterclass against a guy he'll be compared to for the foreseeable future if he's in the MVP race? We'll find out at 6 PM. Be there!

Detroit Pistons (6-2): Cade Cunningham, Duncan Robinson, Ausar Thompson, John Collins, Paul Reed

Los Angeles Lakers (8-2): Luka Dončić, Austin Reaves, Matisse Thybulle, Jake LaRavia, Walker Kessler

#2744. Texas A&M stock report, from Saturday's loss to South Carolina

Texas A&M suffered another frustrating SEC road loss Saturday, falling 17-9 to No. 21 South Carolina at Williams-Brice Stadium despite outgaining the Gamecocks and controlling much of the contest.

The Aggies entered the fourth quarter leading 9-7 but failed to protect their advantage as South Carolina scored 10 unanswered points. Texas A&M dropped to 4-5 overall and 1-5 in SEC play, leaving the team needing two victories in its final three games to become bowl eligible.

Offensive production wasn't the issue, as the Aggies finished with 457 total yards, including 206 rushing yards, while recording 26 first downs. However, missed opportunities, penalties and an inability to finish drives prevented Texas A&M from reaching the end zone.

Several individual performances offered encouragement, particularly in the running game and on defense. Still, the Aggies couldn't turn those efforts into a victory, continuing a troubling pattern against SEC competition.

Here is whose stock rose and fell against South Carolina.

Owens delivered his most productive rushing performance of the season, consistently finding lanes and giving Texas A&M explosive plays. His 44-yard run highlighted an impressive afternoon, but the Aggies couldn't capitalize on his production with a touchdown. Owens averaged more than seven yards per carry and accounted for most of the team's rushing offense.

Stats: 19 carries, 137 yards, 7.2 yards per carry.

Ratcliffe helped anchor a defensive effort that kept South Carolina's offense in check for much of the afternoon. The senior safety contributed in coverage and against the run, helping limit the Gamecocks to just four third-down conversions. His performance was one of the more encouraging aspects of another difficult road loss.

Stats: Six tackles, one pass breakup, one quarterback hurry.

White remained one of Texas A&M's most dependable special teams contributors, delivering another outstanding performance against South Carolina. The senior punter averaged 51.2 yards on four attempts, placing all four punts inside the Gamecocks' 20-yard line without recording a touchback. His longest punt traveled 55 yards, and his ability to flip field position helped keep the Aggies competitive despite their offensive struggles.

Stats: Four punts, 205 yards, 51.2 yards per punt, four inside the 20, long of 55 yards.

Reed completed 25 passes without throwing an interception, but the passing attack struggled to generate touchdowns. Despite throwing for 251 yards, Reed couldn't consistently finish drives, and Texas A&M's offense failed to score a touchdown for the third time in SEC play. The quarterback also struggled to make an impact as a runner.

Stats: 25-of-43 passing, 251 yards, zero touchdowns, zero interceptions / nine carries, eight yards.

Horton led Texas A&M with 78 receiving yards, but his costly drops overshadowed an otherwise productive afternoon. With the Aggies leading 9-7 in the third quarter, Horton dropped a potential touchdown pass on first-and-goal, beginning a disastrous sequence that ended with a missed field goal. He also dropped two passes in the fourth quarter that could have extended drives. Despite leading the team in receiving, Horton's inability to make critical catches contributed to Texas A&M's failure to reach the end zone.

Stats: Five receptions, 78 yards, zero touchdowns, 10 targets.

Texas A&M moved the football effectively between the 20-yard lines but repeatedly failed to finish scoring opportunities. Penalties near the goal line and missed chances forced the Aggies to settle for field goals instead of touchdowns. The inability to capitalize on promising drives ultimately overshadowed an otherwise productive statistical performance.

Stats: One score in three red-zone trips / zero touchdowns / 457 total yards.

#2739. Cleveland Browns vs. New Orleans Saints recap: Shedeur Sanders comes close, but can’t get the final play in overtime

I was hopeful to see QB Shedeur Sanders heading into this game, but it was very ugly for most of the game. Then, down 9-6 with a few minutes to go, he found WR KC Concepcion for a long touchdown pass to put Cleveland on top 13-9. The offense couldn't quite close the game out after that, and then the defense allowed their first touchdown of the day with a minute to go, being down 16-13. An incredible connection to WR Jerry Jeudy set up a 51-yard field goal by K Andre Szmyt to send the game to overtime, and he drilled it to make it 16-16.

Unfortunately, the defense gave up a lengthy touchdown drive in overtime. Cleveland responded with a touchdown drive with a minute to go, and then faced the decision: a possible tie, let the Saints have a chance to win with a field goal, or go for the win with a two-point try. They went for the win, and it didn't work out. Cleveland lost 23-22, and dropped to 5-4 on the season, with Deshaun Watson returning next week.

The Browns got the ball first, and it was a quick three-and-out for QB Shedeur Sanders on a drive that included a false start, no runs by RB Quinshon Judkins, and Sanders getting sacked on 3rd-and-long. Then punted to New Orleans, and despite all their run-game struggles, former Browns RB Audric Estime had three straight runs for 32 yards. Then, down by the goal line, after getting the Saints into a 2nd-and-13, DE Chris Williams and DE Jared Verse jumped into the neutral zone on back-to-back snaps to make it 2nd-and-3.

On 2nd-and-3, the handoff to RB Alvin Kamara led to a muff and a loss of 5 yards. On 3rd-and-8, QB Tyler Shough tried to scramble after not finding anyone, but LB Carson Schwesinger darted in and sacked him for a loss of 2 yards to force a field goal. K Charlie Smyth hit from 30 yards out to give the Saints a 3-0 lead.

The Browns began their second drive at their own 27 yard line. This time, they handed it off to Judkins for a pickup of 4 yards. A quick screen to WR KC Concepcion then moved the chains. A few plays later, on 3rd-and-9, a crossing route to WR Denzel Boston only got 7 yards, leading to a punt by the Browns. P Corey Bojorquez got his punt downed at the 7 yard line with about five Browns around it, but of course, the player who touched it (S Daniel Thomas) was flagged for illegal touching (he went out of bounds and was first to touch it), leading to a re-kick.

After the re-kick and a Saints return to the 37 yard line, it was a big difference in field position. After a first down pass to WR Chris Olave, Shough took off for 15 yards a couple plays later to avoid a sack, as individual mistakes were running rampant across the team. That included S Grant Delpit two plays later, as he was flagged for pass interference to put the ball at the Browns' 29 yard line. Two runs by Estime set up 3rd-and-5. DT Mike Hall came up with the sack up the middle on Shough, pushing the Saints back to the 34 yard line. Smyth's attempt was now from 52 yards out, and it was pushed to the right and no good.

After the missed field goal, the Browns took over at their own 42 yard line with 8 seconds left in the quarter. Sanders ran a playfake from Shotgun, had plenty of time, but rolled to his left, and then had his pass tipped and incomplete.

A pitch play Judkins got 6 yards to set up 3rd-and-4, and Sanders got RB Dylan Sampson wide open in the flat to pick up a first down and get into Saints territory. Sanders avoided a free rusher on second down to throw the ball away, and then on third down, the Saints were finally called for a penalty via illegal contact to give Cleveland a fresh set of downs.

Two runs by Sampson set up a 3rd-and-3, something looked off as Sanders quickly went up the middle and was stopped for 1 yard — it didn't look like it should've been a quarterback draw, especially since Todd Monken looked animated on the sidelines as he sent the field goal unit out. K Andre Szmyt came on and connected from 41 yards out to tie the game at 3-3.

Shough laid out a beautiful deep ball to WR Barion Brown for 52 yards, beating S Ronnie Hickman.

Two plays later, WR Jaylon Tyson made the first catch of his NFL career, and lunged toward the end zone, but Schwesinger punched it out for a fumble, and CB Tyson Campbell recovered for Cleveland kept it at the 1-yard line.

To avoid a safety, Sanders did a quarterback sneak to gain 4 yards. Judkins got the next handoff for 5 yards, setting up 3rd-and-1. Another handoff to Judkins got the first down. A few plays later, on 3rd-and-6, Sanders tried to escape the pocket, but was chased down from behind after a 1 yard gain, forcing another punt.

On the punt, Brown tried to reverse field to get more yards, but he ended up going backwards, and then DT Adin Huntington tackled him and forced a fumble, and S Donovan McMillian recovered at the Saints' 19 yard line.

Sampson carried for 1 yard, and on 2nd-and-9, the Saints jumped offsides to make it 2nd-and-4. The end around went to Concepcion, and he was able to squeeze three yards out with limited space to make it 3rd-and-1. Sanders handed to Judkins, and this time there was no miscommunication, as he got the yard to set up 1st-and-goal at the 9 yard line heading into the two-minute warning.

Sanders ran a playaction fake, but the edge defender wasn't fooled by the threat of a run, and got an easy sack on Sanders for a loss of 6 yards. On 2nd-and-goal from the 15 yard line, they handed to Judkins, and he found an opening for 11 yards to make it 3rd-and-goal at the 4 yard line. Sanders ran a quicker playaction fake, then took off up the middle for 3 yards to make it 4th-and-goal. Monken opted to go for it, and Sanders bumped into his lineman before handing it off, then gave to Judkins, and he was stopped a half yard short with 1:38 to go, keeping it a tie game at 3-3.

Now the Browns' defense needed to seek out a safety opportunity. Shough tried to sneak it on first down, but got no gain, as Cleveland took their first timeout. On second down, Shough hit Olave on the outside for 7 yards, making it 3rd-and-3. Shough lofted it for Olave up the right side, and he made the catch with CB Myles Harden draped all over him for a gain of 35 yards.

The defense came up with a stop after that, but only 27 seconds left. The Saints punted to Concepcion, and it was fair caught at the 9 yard line. Cleveland kneeled it out from there to send it to halftime.

New Orleans got the ball to start the second half and began at the 36 yard line. Two runs to Estimate made it 3rd-and-5, and Shough tried to hit Olave again, but Harden tipped the pass away to force a punt. The punt went out of bounds at the 22 yard line, where Sanders would get his first crack at second half redemption.

After two run plays by Judkins, it was 3rd-and-6. Sanders scrambled to his left and ran for 11 yards and a first down. On the next play, Sanders finally aired one out deep for Boston. Even though it was underthrown, Boston high-pointed the ball and got yards after the catch for 60 yards, down to the 3 yard line.

Unfortunately, things went backwards from there. Judkins was stuffed for a loss of 2 yards, then Sanders was drilled for a sack that lost 7 yards. After a third down incompletion, Szmyt came on and was good from 30 yards out to give the Browns their first lead of the day at 6-3 with 9:01 left in the thrid quarter.

Brown got another return out to the 37 yard line to begin New Orleans' next drive. A misdirection playfake led to a first down pass to TE Noah Fant near midfield. A couple plays later, Estime found a little burst for 8 yards to get into field goal range. Shough then found an opening for the second time of the day, scrambling for 11 yards and another first down. LB Quincy Williams made a good tackle on Olave to set up 3rd-and-7. Shough got away from DE Derek Barnett and ran for another first down.

The defense held tough once again in the red zone, as Shough tried to bail outside the pocket again, but was stopped by Schwesinger for a short sack. Smyth hit a 27 yard field goal to tie the game at 6-6 with 2:26 left in the third quarter.

Cleveland tried coming out with a misdirection screen pass, but it was knocked down by a defensive lineman. A couple plays later, Sanders was sacked on third down, leading to a punt. Rinse and repeat, the Saints would begin another drive at the 37 yard line after the return by Brown. The defense got the stop again, as Harden came on a blitz untouched to sack Shough for a loss of 10 yards on the final play of the quarter.

Concepcion fair caught the ball at the 23 yard line to begin the fourth quarter, and then Judkins started with a 2-yard run. On second down, Sanders hit Sampson on a swing pass for a gain of 10 yards and a first down. A 5-yard run by Sampson, and then a quick comeback to Concepcion, got the ball to midfield.

A couple plays later, Sanders' swing pass to Sanders was tipped and incomplete, making it 3rd-and-7. Sanders scrambled to the sideline and out of bounds, leading to a punt attempt. On the punt, the Saints were offsides, and Monken sent the offense back out for a 4th-and-2 at the Saints' 42 yard line. Sanders had no idea where to go, rolled to his left, and then threw the ball out of bounds for a turnover on downs with 10:32 left in the game.

The Saints faced a 3rd-and-3 at midfield, and Shough hit Tyson on the quick out for a first down. On another third down, Tyson caught a pass short of the first down, setting up 4th-and-1 at the Browns' 37 yard line. The Saints went for it and were stopped, but Campbell was flagged for illegal contact, giving New Orleans a first down.

Harden blitzed again on second down and sacked Shough for a loss of 6 yards, making it 3rd-and-16 at the 38 yard line. Shough avoided a sack on third down and was able to get back into field goal range. Smyth came on from 48 yards out, and the kick was good to put the Saints back on top 9-6 with 5:38 left in the game.

Bond's return was taken out to the 36 yard line. Then, the deep ball came back again — Concepcion beat former Browns CB Martin Emerson, caught it, and then went across the entire field for a 64-yard touchdown pass to put the Browns up 13-9 with 5:21 to go.

With the Saints stunned, could the Browns' defense continue to keep them off the board to close out the game? A run by Shough set up a 3rd-and-3, and he couldn't find his receiver on the sideline in time, leading to an incomplete pass. The Saints had a decision to make, and they opted to bring the punt unit out with 4:23 to go. Concepcion made the fair catch at the 16 yard line, with the offense now trying to close out the game.

They gave it to Judkins to start the drive for a gain of 4 yards. On second down, Judkins got 2 more yards to set up 3rd-and-4. Sanders took the snap, and took off up the middle for 5 yards and a first down, as the Saints burned their first timeout.

The drive went backwards after that, with a holding penalty on LG Zion Johnson, and Sanders being sacked for a loss of 8 yards. They ran the ball twice to head to the two-minute warning with a punt formation at their own 16 yard line, and the Saints having no timeout remaining.

Brown returned the Saints' punt to the 45 yard line, needing 55 yards for a touchdown to win. They began with a swing pass to Estime for 6 yards, as he got out of bounds to stop the clock. Shough then tried to hit Olave deep, but Campbell had good coverage and it was incomplete. On third down, Shough found Tyson over the middle for a first down. On the next play, Shough got a perfect pass to Olave this time for a perfect 33-yard completion to the 10-yard line with 1:08 to go.

Shough then hit Kamara over the middle for 8 yards to the 2 yard line, as the Browns now took their first timeout with 1:00 remaining. Shough gave it to Estime, and he took it in for the touchdown to put the Saints back up 16-13, and now the pressure back on Cleveland to need a field goal with 58 seconds left and two timeouts. Bond stumbled on the return, going down at the 25 yard line.

On first down, Concepcion booted a wide open sideline pass that would've gone for about 15 yards. On second down, Sanders hit Boston short for 4 yards, and Cleveland burned their second timeout with 41 seconds left. On third down, Sanders rolled right, was drilled by DE Chase Young, and somehow hit WR Jerry Jeudy for 30 yards to the Saints' 40 yard line, as Cleveland took their final timeout with 30 seconds to go.

Sanders threw an incomplete pass, now with 0:26 left. On second down, Sanders hit Jeudy for 8 yards, and then they clocked it to bring on Szmyt from 51 yards. He drilled it right down the middle to tie the game at 16-16 with 8 seconds to go.

The Saints took a knee after the touchback to send the game to overtime — Cleveland's first overtime game in four years.

The Saints got the ball first in overtime, starting at the 26 yard line. Kamara had a 9 yard run to set up 3rd-and-1, and then moved the chains after that with another run. A 7-yard pass to Olave was followed by a 15-yard run by Kamara to the Browns' 39 yard line. Shough took a first down deep shot to Olave, but CB Denzel Ward had tight coverage on the incompletion. Then, a quick hitter pass over the middle got 9 yards to make it 3rd-and-1. Estime got the quick handoff after that for another 9 yards to the Browns' 21 yard line.

As Shough tried to escape from DT Mason Graham, a hold was called on the Saints, pushing them back to a 1st-and-20 at the 31 yard line. Shough got most of that back with an 8-yard scramble to set up 2nd-and-12. Another quick pass set up 3rd-and-4 at the 15 yard line. Shough found TE Juwan Johnson on the flag to the corner, and the extra point made it 23-16.

Now came the hypotheticals for Cleveland, with 4:17 remaining: you need a touchdown, but if you get it, do you go for two and the win, or the tie? But first, they needed another touchdown drive. Cleveland began at the 33 yard line, and it began with a false start on Jeudy. A checkdown to Sampson only got 1 yard. On 2nd-and-14, Sanders checked it to Boston quickly, and he gained 15 yards for a first down.

A short completion to WR Tylan Wallace set up 3rd-and-4 heading into the two-minute warning at the 50 yard line. Boston moved the chains with a crossing route. Two plays later, they faced 3rd-and-7 at the Saints' 39 yard line with 1:11 to go. Sanders found Fannin, who broke two tackles with stiff arms and went 39 yards for a touchdown!

With a minute to go, and not wanting the Saints to possibly get a field goal, Cleveland went for two to try to get the win. Unfortunately, as soon as a quick decision wasn't made, fans knew it wasn't looking good. Sanders rolled right, but RT Tytus Howard was flagged for holding and Boston couldn't secure the eventual pass in the corner, ending the game with a loss.

QB Shedeur Sanders: 19-of-31 for 297 yards, 1 TD. 10 carries, 28 yards.

RB Quinshon Judkins: 15 carries, 43 yards.

WR KC Concepcion: 4 catches, 85 yards, 1 TD.

TE Harold Fannin: 2 catches, 42 yards, 1 TD.

It was very frustrating in the first half to see the Browns not convert on 4th-and-goal at the 1 yard line, which could've made it a 10-3 game. This isn't just a throwaway game, this is the type of game that could be the difference between making and missing the playoffs, and we dealt with simple operation issues.

I saw some growth from Sanders last year, and was hoping to see a leap in year two. This game made him look like there's been no growth, and some regression, for 3 quarters. I can't use the reps excuse anymore, because this is year two. He let loose more in the fourth quarter out of necessity, and it paid dividends.

Up next, the Browns head home to take on the Houston Texans.
